Among them, a black-faced, tall, and sturdy woman threw her wooden stick up and laughed, "Don't any of you move. Dealing with such a little girl doesn't require such a big show. I'll handle it myself!"

With that, she reached out to grab Ziyun’s shoulder. Ziyun took advantage of the momentum to perform a heavy back-throw. With a muffled "thud," the black-faced woman was thrown heavily to the ground and couldn't get up.

The other women were stunned. No wonder Foreman Yan brought so many of them. This little girl was actually quite formidable!

The women were all used to heavy labor; they were large, strong, and ruthless, often acting as enforcers among the low-level palace maids. They were used to bullying others and had never seen a rebellious maid like Ziyun.

The women were all enraged and swarmed forward, thinking that even if they just used their weight, they could crush the little girl.

Seeing them attacking together, Ziyun dodged their encirclement. The women missed Ziyun, and in their anger and haste, one woman with a rope tried to snare her. Ziyun dodged and lured her away from the group.

Once she was a distance away, Ziyun tripped the woman, who fell face-first. Ziyun then mounted her waist and used the rope to tie her hands behind her back. The woman lay on the ground, unable to rise.

The remaining women were also stunned, but relying on their numbers, they still didn't take Ziyun seriously.

One woman, holding a wooden stick, saw her companion fall and charged at Ziyun, raising the stick.

At this moment, Ziyun was still on the back of the woman on the ground. The woman swung the stick viciously at Ziyun’s head. If it had hit, Ziyun, being mortal, would surely have been in grave danger!

Ziyun leaped away, and the stick hit the arm of the woman on the ground instead. She let out a cry, "Ouch, you hit the wrong person!"

The woman with the stick, seeing she had missed Ziyun, swung a second time.

Ziyun was prepared. She dodged the stick, spotted an opening, and landed an uppercut on the woman’s chin!

The punch was heavy; the woman was dazed and sat down on the ground. Ziyun rushed over, snatched the stick from her hand, and poked her in the chest. The sturdy woman collapsed and couldn't get up.

The remaining three women and Foreman Yan rushed forward together.

Ziyun swung the stick, careful not to hit their faces or vital parts, knowing they had no martial arts training and were relying on brute force. She swept the stick at their feet, and with a clever flick, all three women fell to the ground.

Ziyun hit each of their backsides three times with the stick and asked, "Do you know how powerful I am now?"

The women were in great pain and, knowing they were no match for the girl, cried out in unison, "We know! Spare us, Miss!"

Two of the women, who were not yet convinced and not in too much pain, scrambled up and lunged at Ziyun again.

Ziyun remained calm and hit each of them on the lower leg with the stick. Both women fell to the ground again and dared not move.

Seeing that all the fierce women brought by Foreman Yan were beaten to the ground, Ziyun said to Xiaocui and Wenjuan, "Go close the gate. Don't let anyone in."

Xiaocui and Wenjuan immediately closed the gate.

They had seen the women come in with sticks and ropes and thought Ziyun would certainly be beaten. They hadn't expected them all to be defeated by Ziyun. Their hearts had been pounding, and they had been truly worried for her. Seeing this outcome, they finally relaxed and felt happy for Ziyun.

They quickly closed the gate, wondering how Ziyun would deal with the aftermath.

These women were not to be trifled with; in this small environment, they were not only enforcers but also bullies.

They closed the gate and looked at Ziyun, feeling very afraid, not knowing how much trouble Ziyun had caused this time.

chapters.title: Fighting Fire with Fire
chapters.content:
Ziyun, bold and courageous, picked up the wooden stick and returned to Foreman Yan’s chair with a calm expression. She sat down and said to the old women lying on the ground, "You bunch of ignorant old things, all of you, sit up!"

The five women sat up, not daring to move. They had been beaten into submission and were now very obedient.

The woman whose hands were tied behind her back said, "I can't sit up."

Ziyun said to Foreman Yan, "Go and untie her."

Foreman Yan, now also very obedient, hurried over to untie the rope. The woman remained sprawled on the ground, refusing to get up.

Seeing her feigning helplessness, Ziyun said to Foreman Yan, "Move aside!"

Foreman Yan stepped aside.

Ziyun walked over and struck the woman on the buttocks with the stick. The woman jumped up in pain and obediently sat down with the others.

"Xiaocui, bring me a chair. I want to teach them my rules!"

"Yes!" Xiaocui immediately brought over the chair Foreman Yan had been sitting on.

After sitting down, Ziyun said to the women, "You bunch of ignorant fools, do you know who I am?"

The women shook their heads.

"You don't? Fine, let me tell you. I am the daughter of the Wei family. I only ended up in this miserable state because I refused to become a concubine for Lord Yang. That is why I am being bullied by you. If I were to change my mind and agree to marry Lord Yang, I would be your mistress. Do you understand?"

"We understand. We were blind and failed to recognize a person of importance. We have offended you, and we beg for your forgiveness!" said one of the women who was quick-witted.

"Young lady, we didn't know you were Lord Yang's person. Ignorance is no crime. Now that we know, we will never cause you trouble again," another added.

Foreman Yan was most interested in what Ziyun had said last. Forgetting her own pain, she asked, "Young lady, when you change your mind, we will be sure to pay our respects to you."

Ziyun sneered, "That will require me to think it over carefully."

"Yes, yes, young lady. This is a life-changing matter; you must think it over," Foreman Yan fawned.

"Keep your mouth shut! Is my personal business something you can just blather about?" Ziyun snapped.

"I deserve to die! My mouth must have been filled with filth today to be so foul and displease you. I deserve to die, I deserve to die!" Foreman Yan now appeared servile and fawning, her former arrogance completely swept away.

"I have a question for you," Ziyun asked coldly. "If I agree to be with Lord Yang, would beating you ignorant old hags to death be as trivial as stepping on a bedbug?"

"Yes, yes," the women replied timidly, terrified of being beaten.

"Are you all afraid of death?" Ziyun asked, raising the stick in her hand.

"We are afraid of death! Please show mercy!" Foreman Yan was also afraid. If this girl really did marry Lord Yang, her life would be in the girl's hands. She had no choice but to be afraid.

"As long as you fear death, that's fine. There are two paths before you: one is to be beaten to death by me, and the other is to help me with my work. Choose for yourselves."

Ziyun stared at them with a stern gaze.

The women immediately replied, "We'll work, we'll work."

"Good. Are you all truly willing to help me with my work?"

"Yes, yes, young lady. We were blind before and offended you. We can work. It is our honor that you would ask us to work for you. Please calm your anger and tell us what to do," one woman said, immediately trying to curry favor.

"Actually, it's nothing much. It's just the work I usually do, which you delayed today. I'm fining each of you 50 night-soil buckets to wash. You have one hour. Can you do it?" Ziyun asked.

When they heard they had to scrub night-soil buckets, some agreed, while others remained silent. Foreman Yan, in particular, found this even more humiliating than being slapped in the face.

Besides, she couldn't bring herself to lose face like that.

Seeing that some were reluctant, Ziyun raised her stick and said, "If you don't want to wash the buckets, that's fine. One strike of the stick equals five buckets. Ten strikes equal 50 buckets. Whoever isn't afraid of having their buttocks beaten to a pulp doesn't have to wash them."

"We women all washed night-soil buckets when we first entered the palace. A little work is nothing," one woman said, fearing a beating, and she went off to start scrubbing.

The other women, including Foreman Yan, also feared the stick and went to wash the buckets.

All 300 buckets were scrubbed clean in less than an hour and hung on the wooden stakes.

This terrified Wenjuan and Xiaocui. What were they to do? With no work left to do, they were at a loss.

Ziyun saw this and said to them, "I take full responsibility for my actions; it has nothing to do with you two. I will bear the consequences. You don't need to worry."

She then turned to Foreman Yan and said, "Everything that happened today and will happen in the future has nothing to do with them, right?"

"Right," Foreman Yan said. "It has nothing to do with them. They truly did not participate in this."

"All of you, come here!" Ziyun called them over and said, "I have one more thing to tell you. Since you've helped me, you must help me to the end."

Ziyun watched their reactions; they were angry but dared not speak.

"From now on," Ziyun said, "you will come here every day. Each of you must scrub 50 buckets to be finished. Otherwise, every time I see you, I will give you ten strikes of the stick."

The women dared not make a sound.

"Will you come or not?" Ziyun demanded.

The women now knew Ziyun's status. If she really did become Lord Yang's concubine, they wouldn't even be able to get close to her if they wanted to curry favor.

This girl was not to be trifled with; they had no choice but to submit.

"Tomorrow, after breakfast, I will come," one woman finally said.

Soon after, all the women agreed to come the next day to scrub the buckets. Foreman Yan had no choice but to follow suit.

"Good. I'll let you go now. Whoever doesn't show up tomorrow, watch out for the stick!" With that, she stood up and performed a set of stick techniques in the open space, leaving Foreman Yan and the others dazzled and stunned with fear.

"You may go," Ziyun said, putting away the stick.

Xiaocui and Wenjuan quickly opened the gate to let the women out.

As soon as they were outside, one woman began cursing Foreman Yan, who had to try to appease them.

One woman said to Foreman Yan, "You wash my 50 buckets every day!"

Another said, "This is all your fault, so my 50 buckets are yours too!"

All five women demanded that Foreman Yan do their share.

She couldn't possibly do it alone, so she said to them, "This is all my fault, and I apologize. We've been colleagues for years; you wouldn't leave me to die, would you?"

"How do you propose we save you?" one asked.

"How about this? Every day, you come here and work for one hour, and I will pay you in copper coins."

When they heard there was money to be made, they all said, "Fine!"

"How many coins?" one asked.

"Ten coins each."

"Heh," one woman laughed, "it has to be at least 30."

After some haggling, they settled on 20 copper coins per shift, paid daily.

From then on, the six women came every day to scrub the buckets.

Ziyun cleared a space and practiced martial arts every day, while Xiaocui and Wenjuan watched, doing nothing.

Foreman Yan no longer dared to bully them.

With others helping to wash the buckets, the three girls enjoyed a period of peace.

Ziyun turned 18 without realizing it. Lord Yang received word that Ziyun's attitude had softened.

Lord Yang believed his judgment was correct; in another half a year, Ziyun would willingly submit to him. However, he never dreamed that something else was happening within the palace.

Although Emperor Xuanzong spent his days with the "Four Lis", Li Bai, Li Guinian, Li Henian, and Li Pengnian, keeping Consort Yang happy with endless feasting, music, and dance, he learned that the soldiers stationed at the Muci Mountain border lacked winter uniforms. He immediately ordered the women of the six palaces and his concubines to sew winter battle robes to comfort the troops and boost morale.

All the women in the palace were given materials to sew the robes. The 3,000 palace maids were each tasked with sewing five robes.

Ziyun and her two companions were also given cloth, cotton, and needles, with orders to finish within a month.

The robes came in large, medium, and small sizes, with specific patterns and materials provided.

Xiaocui got the small size, Wenjuan the medium, and Ziyun the large.

Ziyun made the first four robes according to the standard patterns and sizes. When making the last one, they had plenty of cotton and cloth left over, enough to make an extra-large robe.

Ziyun gathered the leftover materials and made an extra-large robe, one that would fit a tall, sturdy warrior.

The three maids put on the robes they had made, laughing and playing. They felt they had done something meaningful.

Ziyun showed the extra-large robe to Xiaocui and Wenjuan. "What do you think? Big enough?"

They both agreed it was huge.

"This wide, thick robe is perfect for a tall, burly general," Wenjuan said.

Xiaocui added, "Someone at least six feet tall would have to wear it; a short person couldn't."

She touched the hem and said, "It's so thick; it must be very warm."

Ziyun took a brush and ink and wrote a small poem on a scrap of paper: "Muci Mountain, Muci Mountain, Tang soldiers guard the frontier. Heaven and earth are cold, swords are icy, the Emperor sends warmth in these robes. More thread, more cotton, who will wear this extra-large robe? I hate that in this life, we have no fate, I will wait for you in the next life."

After writing it, she folded it into a small square, tucked it into a corner of the collar, and stitched it shut.

Xiaocui asked, "What will the person who gets this robe think when they see this note?"

"They'll be secretly happy. I think they'll fight bravely and repay us with military merit," Ziyun said.

"Did you write the note because you want to meet the person who gets the robe?" Xiaocui asked.

"That's just wishful thinking. There are constant battles at the border; who knows when they might die on the battlefield?"

"War means death. The soldiers at the border are so pitiful. If we didn't make these robes for them, how would they survive the winter!" Wenjuan sighed.

"I hope that whoever wears the robes we sewed will have good luck, fight bravely, win honors, and return home safely," Ziyun prayed.

Whenever the border soldiers were mentioned, the three girls prayed for their safety.

Speaking of returning home, Ziyun asked Xiaocui and Wenjuan, "Will we ever be able to leave here alive?"

"Can't we?" Wenjuan asked.

"We've been here for over a year. Have you ever heard of a palace maid leaving the palace?" Ziyun asked.

Wenjuan and Xiaocui shook their heads.

"None, right? I asked Foreman Yan, and she hasn't heard of it either. It seems we can get in, but we can't get out! We'll all grow old and die here." From the first day she entered the palace, Ziyun had never intended to stay long; she had always been thinking of leaving.

"I knew when I came in that palace maids couldn't leave. Since we're here, we might as well settle down," Wenjuan said.

When she entered, her family had told her about the situation for palace maids.

"Does the note you wrote mean," Xiaocui asked, "that you hope to meet the person who gets the extra-large robe in this life?"

"In the next life," Wenjuan answered for Ziyun. "In the next life, maybe you'll meet, right?"

"Hmm," Ziyun said. "Whether we meet in the next life isn't important. What matters is the sentiment. I hope we all have a next life, and in that life, we can all get everything we wanted in this one."

"Yes," Wenjuan agreed. "And I hope to see the soldiers who wore the robes I sewed, to see the heroic scene of them returning in triumph after winning the war."

Xiaocui was suddenly inspired. "I'll write a note and sew it in too."

Wenjuan said, "I'll write one too."

"Have you decided what to write?" Ziyun asked.

"I'm thinking," Xiaocui said.

"I've decided." Wenjuan picked up her brush and began to write.

"Hand over the work! Bring the finished robes along with the leftover cotton and cloth, quickly!" A eunuch shouted as he approached, collecting all the robes they had made.

Wenjuan hadn't had a chance to sew her note in, and Xiaocui hadn't even written hers yet. All 15 robes were taken away by the eunuch.

Ziyun watched as the eunuch carried away the robe with her note inside, her heart pounding.

She wasn't afraid of the note being discovered; she knew perfectly well that since it was stitched into the collar, the eunuch would never find it. Of that, she was certain.

She was wondering: into whose hands would the note fall? A general? A soldier? Was he brave in battle? Had he been wounded? Would he die on the battlefield?

From that day on, Ziyun carried a new burden in her heart.

chapters.title: Yan Zhenqing Inspects the Granary (1)
chapters.content:
After Wei Zhuoqing settled his wife and son in Changshan, he was introduced to Yan Zhenqing by Yan Gaoqing. At the time, Yan Zhenqing was serving as the Governor of Pingyuan, and people referred to him as "Governor Yan of Pingyuan."

Wei Zhuoqing greatly admired the calligraphy of the Governor of Pingyuan, particularly its bold strength and transcendent, otherworldly quality.

The Governor of Pingyuan had been demoted to this region due to the persecution of Yang Guozhong. Upon learning of Wei Zhuoqing’s plight, he felt a sense of shared destiny and deep sympathy for him, while harboring intense resentment toward the Yang family for their manipulation of the imperial court and their oppression of the people.

He said to Wei Zhuoqing, "Since you have settled your family in Changshan, you must be extremely careful. Keep your lips sealed and do not let any information leak out; the Yang family’s spies are everywhere. While I am in Pingyuan, I can provide you with a position that keeps you out of the public eye."

"Can a government post really keep one out of the public eye?" Wei Zhuoqing asked.

"This position will absolutely ensure you remain hidden. In Dahuagou, there is a large granary that stores enough grain and fodder to feed fifty thousand troops. The previous keeper was imprisoned for selling off the grain. I hope you will take over and manage this granary well."

"Where is Dahuagou?" Wei Zhuoqing asked, thinking to himself that the name suggested a location deep in a mountain ravine. If it were truly in a ravine, he could live under an assumed name and avoid public scrutiny.

"It is in a deep mountain ravine ten miles from the city, completely isolated by nature. The advantage for you is that this granary is cut off from the world. As long as you do not want outsiders to know you are there, no one will. Is Magistrate Wei willing to accept this humble post?"

"Many thanks, Governor Yan. This humble servant will certainly manage the granary well for you! At the same time, I can devote myself to studying your calligraphy. I believe the Yang family’s control over the court will not last long; we will eventually have our day."

Wei Zhuoqing was deeply grateful for the Governor’s care. He gladly accepted the post and took up his duties shortly thereafter.

The previous keepers of this granary had all met with disaster due to the illicit sale of military grain. Because the granary was far from the magistrate's office and lacked long-term supervision, the keepers often found themselves in prison or even beheaded for their negligence.

The Governor of Pingyuan had been fretting over finding someone of reliable character to manage the facility when Wei Zhuoqing appeared. Since he was a close friend of Yan Gaoqing, his character was surely sound. After learning of his circumstances, the Governor felt even more certain that he was the right man for the job, and he felt at ease handing the granary over to him.

Once Wei Zhuoqing had settled his family, he entrusted someone to inquire about news of Miss Ziyun in the palace. Upon learning that his daughter was performing menial tasks in the Xingqing Palace, he felt relieved; as long as she was in the palace and away from the harassment of the Yang tyrant, he was content.

The Wei family had finally escaped disaster and settled down without further loss. After taking office, Wei Zhuoqing realized the Governor’s thoughtful intentions: the granary was nestled in a mountain hollow with only one road leading to the outside world. Once the gate was closed, it was completely cut off from society.

This was a strategic reserve granary intended for emergency use during wartime.

The Governor of Pingyuan personally escorted him to the warehouse, announced the appointment, and introduced him to the deputy keeper, Zhang Jiang.

Zhang Jiang was an honest and loyal man, upright in his conduct, and had not participated in the previous keeper’s grain-selling schemes.

After taking office, Wei Zhuoqing compared the ledgers and conducted a thorough audit of the inventory to determine the extent of the deficit.

The previous keeper had been incredibly bold; of the fifty large warehouses, half were empty. Because of his poor management, the granary was infested with rats, and he had blamed the shortages on the vermin.

Wei Zhuoqing brought in a group of local cats and even invented a "Wei-style" mousetrap. Within half a year, the rats in the warehouse were completely eradicated.

In his spare time, Wei Zhuoqing practiced Yan Zhenqing’s calligraphy to find solace in his remaining days.

"Magistrate Wei, your calligraphy is magnificent!" Zhang Jiang exclaimed, watching Wei practice.

"Not at all, not at all. It is far inferior to the Governor’s," Wei Zhuoqing replied. He was not being modest; how could his writing compare to Yan Zhenqing’s? He knew it would be difficult to ever catch up.

"Heh heh, I’m not a learned man, but I’ve seen the Governor’s writing, and it looks about the same as yours. They’re both square and upright characters," Zhang Jiang said.

"It doesn't matter if you don't understand it. Whether the calligraphy is good or not doesn't affect the fighting. Defending this granary depends on the blade in your hand, not the brush in mine," Wei Zhuoqing said.

"These are peaceful times," Zhang Jiang remarked. "There are no battles to fight. I long to fight on the battlefield and achieve glory, but there are so few wars in our dynasty. Look at these past few years, the weather has been favorable, the harvests are bountiful, there are no major conflicts at the borders, and the people live in peace and contentment."

"This grain reserve has never been used. Every year, we have to replace the old grain with new. I have all this martial skill, but nowhere to use it."

"Please remember an old saying: 'Raise an army for a thousand days to use it for a single moment.' Do not be anxious; opportunities will come. Just be prepared," Wei Zhuoqing said.

"Haha, Magistrate Wei is trying to comfort me. Although Yang Guozhong controls the court, he wouldn't dare rebel. The country is stable, and the borders are secure."

"Even if there are occasional incursions by foreign tribes, it’s not enough to satisfy the border troops. Peace is good, peace is truly good!" Although Zhang Jiang knew it was difficult for an uneducated junior officer like him to rise to the rank of general during peacetime, he did not truly wish for war.

War would be different. If he fought a few major battles and earned enough merit, he could realize his dream of becoming a general, provided he didn't die in the process. But when war breaks out, the common people suffer the most; so many lives are ruined, and families are destroyed. It is better to have no war.

"Well said. A warrior loves peace. But tell me, do you think the situation in the imperial court is looking a bit ominous?" Wei Zhuoqing asked.

"Ominous? What is ominous?"

Zhang Jiang was merely a deputy granary keeper; how could he understand the grand affairs of the court?

Seeing his confusion, Wei Zhuoqing explained: "Because Lady Yang is favored, her entire family has risen to power. Not only that, but Yang Guozhong monopolizes the government, excludes those who disagree with him, and kills the innocent! The entire court and the public are filled with complaints."

"I fear this will lead to internal strife. Once internal strife begins, it means war, and the ones who will suffer are the common people. Think about it, does that make sense?"

"Hmm, the talk about the Yang family is rampant; I’ve heard plenty. If Yang Guozhong keeps going like this, there will surely be a great disaster. Hasn't the Emperor noticed?" Zhang Jiang asked.

"The Emperor is currently soaked in Lady Yang’s 'soul-stealing soup.' He can neither hear loyal advice nor see the true reality. Alas, a once-wise monarch is being ruined by a beauty!" Wei Zhuoqing sighed.

"Is it really that serious?" Zhang Jiang asked.

"Think back through history, how many monarchs have been ruined by women?" Wei Zhuoqing countered.

He was deeply worried that Emperor Xuanzong would be destroyed in Lady Yang’s gentle dream. But what use was his worry?

A year later, the Governor of Pingyuan arrived with his entourage to inspect the granary. Wei Zhuoqing first led him to inspect the city defenses; the walls were sturdy, the equipment was well-maintained, and the soldiers were healthy and spirited. The Governor was very satisfied.

Then, they inspected the grain warehouses. The grain was plentiful, the quality was well-preserved, and the facilities were complete. There were no rats to be seen, and the Governor was pleased.

When the Governor noticed several cats in each warehouse, he asked Wei Zhuoqing, "Are these cats yours?"

"In response to your inquiry, Governor, there was once a rat infestation here. Since we started keeping cats, the rats have moved out. Now, there is no vermin damage in the granaries."

"Magistrate Wei, you govern with great skill. Let us have a drink tonight. What dishes have you prepared to go with the wine?"

The Governor was testing him to see if he would take this opportunity to host a lavish banquet and squander public funds.

"In response to your inquiry, Governor, since this is your first time drinking here, I must fulfill my duties as a host. I have already instructed the kitchen to prepare a grand banquet to welcome you and your party," Wei Zhuoqing said.

Hearing the words "grand banquet," the Governor felt a bit displeased, but he wanted to see just how grand a banquet this Wei Zhuoqing could throw. Could it be that he had misjudged him, and that he was just as vulgar as his predecessor? Though unhappy, he followed Wei Zhuoqing to a large warehouse.

It turned out that Wei Zhuoqing had set up the "grand banquet" inside the warehouse.

Upon entering, the Governor saw a long table eight feet wide and over ten zhang long, covered with a tablecloth. Chairs were arranged on both sides, enough to seat over a hundred people.

Wei Zhuoqing invited the Governor of Pingyuan to the seat of honor and asked his entourage to be seated. Then, he called for the deputy keeper and the guards to enter.

As they entered, they respectfully paid their respects to the Governor.

The Governor still could not tell what Wei Zhuoqing was up to. Being a man who respected the virtuous and cared for his soldiers, he signaled for everyone to be seated.

"Thank you, Governor!" the soldiers shouted in unison, their voices booming. They then took their seats in an orderly fashion.

"Well-trained and disciplined," the Governor thought, a faint smile appearing on his face.

At that moment, a young soldier with a baby face came to serve tea to the Governor: "Governor, please have some tea."

He was a new recruit who had joined this year. Having never been in such a formal setting, he was extremely nervous. After speaking, his face turned red, and cold sweat broke out on his forehead.

The Governor took an immediate liking to the young soldier. As a governor who loved his troops like his own children, he saw the boy’s nervousness and quickly said, "Don't be nervous. How old are you?"

"Nineteen." He was so nervous that he forgot all the polite phrases Wei Zhuoqing had taught him, and not knowing where to put his hands, he nervously clutched the corner of his uniform.

"Are you betrothed?" the Governor asked with a smile, hoping to lighten the tense atmosphere.

"No, not yet."

Someone in the back giggled.

"How long have you been in the granary guard?" the Governor asked.

"This year, I just... just arrived." As he said this, he suddenly remembered something and added, "I forgot something."

The Governor smiled and asked, "What is it? Tell me, don't be nervous."

"I... I didn't tell you what kind of tea this is."

The atmosphere relaxed, and the young soldier was no longer as nervous, finally remembering what he was supposed to say.

"Is this fine tea from Magistrate Wei’s own home?" The Governor felt a flicker of displeasure again, assuming Wei Zhuoqing had instructed the soldier to claim it was his private tea to both flatter the Governor and show off his own integrity.

But the young soldier said, "In response to your inquiry, Governor, it is not our Magistrate’s own tea; our Magistrate has no tea of his own." He had just remembered the polite phrasing.

Hearing this, the Governor lifted the lid of the cup; it was a tea made of chrysanthemum and hawthorn.

"If it isn't Magistrate Wei’s, then where did it come from?" the Governor asked gently.

The young soldier continued, "In response to your inquiry, Governor, we grew the chrysanthemums ourselves; there is a large patch on the mountain; the hawthorn grows on the mountain; and we keep the bees ourselves. Our Magistrate says this is a tea that stimulates the appetite and is good for health."

"Appetizing and healthy tea, haha, good! Does everyone have some?" The Governor was pleased; this Wei Zhuoqing was playing a riddle with him.

"In response to your inquiry, Governor, we boiled a large pot, and everyone has some." The young soldier was no longer nervous and answered fluently.

Hearing that they had boiled a large pot, the Governor stood up happily, patted the young soldier on the shoulder, and said, "Your Magistrate is stingy! You boiled a whole pot and only gave me this tiny bowl? Are you feeding a cat? Change it to a large bowl!"

"Yes, sir! Change to a large bowl!" The crowd cheered and applauded, immediately replacing the fine porcelain cups with large, coarse ceramic bowls.

Seeing that every soldier present was served a large bowl of tea, the Governor knew the young soldier wasn't lying. They really had boiled a large pot, which not only whetted his appetite but also piqued his curiosity.

He asked, "Magistrate Wei, you also keep bees?"

"In response to your inquiry, Governor, we keep over fifty hives," Wei Zhuoqing said. "It’s like this: we have a few soldiers here who kept bees at home. Seeing the mountain covered in wildflowers, they suggested I keep bees."

"Our honey is self-produced and consumed. To ensure fairness, we often boil honey tea for everyone to drink. I have prepared a jar for you, Governor, to take back for your family to taste."

"Then why didn't I see the beehives?" the Governor asked.

"In response to your inquiry, Governor, they are all on the mountain. If you stay for a few more days and look outside the wall, you will not only see the beehives but also the fields we have planted. We have grain and various vegetables, and we also raise chickens, pigs, sheep, and fish."

"Good! For that alone, I must go and take a look."

"Governor," Wei Zhuoqing said, "this is a land of great fortune! There are green mountains, forests on the hills, and a stream in the ravine that flows all year round. On both sides of the stream is fertile land."

"We built a large dam downstream where we can raise many fish, ducks, and geese. In wartime, this is our secret weapon. If our first line of defense is breached by the enemy, this dam will become their watery grave."

"Brilliant!" the Governor praised. "I saw this dam on my way here. You and I thought of the same thing, haha! I didn't expect you to know military strategy and be so good at utilizing the terrain. Once this dam is opened, it will be like a mountain flood, ensuring that invaders never return!"

"You flatter me, Governor. I don't know military strategy; this is all Zhang Jiang’s credit. He is not only skilled in martial arts but also well-versed in military tactics," Wei Zhuoqing said, strongly recommending Zhang Jiang to the Governor.

"Him?" the Governor said. "You don't need to tell me; he has long had a place in my heart. It is only a pity that there is no war for him to fight; it is a waste of his talents."

Zhang Jiang gave a shy laugh and said nothing. He was not a man of many words and had even less to say in front of his superiors.

By recommending his deputy to the Governor, Wei Zhuoqing left a very good impression; he was clearly a man who knew how to handle officialdom and people. At the same time, he won the hearts of his subordinates.

"You have to grow grain, vegetables, and raise livestock, where does the labor come from?" the Governor asked.

"In response to your inquiry, Governor, everyone in the granary, including the guards, participates in production. We reward based on labor. The more one contributes, the more one is rewarded."

"Everyone is full of energy. There isn't much work in the warehouse, and being idle leads to trouble. With so many people living in this ravine, if they had nothing to do, they would cause trouble and fight. Working helps stabilize morale and the military spirit."

"With work to do and a harvest to reap, we improve everyone’s meals so that they can eat well."

"You are far from the city. If you didn't grow your own crops and raise livestock to enrich your tables, relying only on the court’s meager silver would make life very difficult," the Governor said, showing he was well aware of the situation on the ground.

"Yes, Governor," Wei Zhuoqing said. "Since we started our own production, everyone in the granary, including the families living here, can eat their fill of staple foods. For side dishes, we have one meat and one vegetable every day; we have meat every single day."

"On the first of every month, we have a small improvement, and on the fifteenth, a major one. Your visit to inspect the granary happens to fall on the fifteenth, so you’ve caught our major improvement."

"So, Magistrate Wei, you mean to say that I’ve arrived at the right time to catch your major improvement, is that it?"

Yan Zhenqing found it hard to believe. While he trusted Wei Zhuoqing’s character and knew he was a good official, he couldn't quite believe they could eat their fill of grain. The court’s rations were barely enough to keep soldiers fed; eating as much as they wanted would surely not be enough. As a man who led troops, he knew exactly how these things worked.

He truly wanted to see how Wei Zhuoqing managed to improve the meals for his officers and soldiers.

chapters.title: Yan Zhenqing Inspects the Granary (2)
chapters.content:
"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "you have arrived at a very opportune moment. We are holding a 'Grand Improvement' event today. We began preparations on the 13th and 14th, slaughtering pigs, sheep, chickens, and geese, catching fish, grinding tofu, and even sending soldiers up the mountain to forage for mushrooms and local produce."

"Oh?" Lord Yan laughed. "It seems this banquet wasn't prepared specifically for me, then!"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "if you had intended to visit, you should have sent a messenger ahead to inform me so that I could have made proper preparations."

"Haha," Lord Yan laughed. "I did it specifically to catch you off guard, to see the state of your defenses and living conditions. I have inspected the defenses along the way; they are acceptable, barely passing."

"You have a unique advantage here: a natural mountain pass that is easy to defend and difficult to attack. It is truly a place where one man can hold the pass against ten thousand. If you cannot secure the granary with such a barrier, you would be the most foolish man in this dynasty."

"As for the living conditions, that depends on how this 'Grand Improvement' goes. Well? Should the event begin?" In truth, Lord Yan was skeptical about their "Grand Improvement."

"Bring out the menu!" Wei Zhuoqing immediately ordered.

"Bring out the menu?" Lord Yan thought to himself, This Wei Zhuoqing is interesting. How many dishes could he possibly have to warrant presenting a menu to me? I must see what tricks he has up his sleeve.

At this moment, a young man who looked like a clerk approached, holding a menu. He stepped forward and said to Lord Yan, "Reporting to your Excellency, this is the menu for today's Grand Improvement. Please have a look."

"Haha, let me see." Lord Yan took the menu and saw it was densely written, filling an entire page. There were indeed quite a few dishes.

Looking closer, he saw the menu was written in precise, small regular script, every character vigorous and powerful. Yan Zhenqing thought: This fellow is finding a way to make me teach him calligraphy. He said to Wei Zhuoqing, "Your handwriting has changed style. It is good; you have made great progress."

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing explained, "this menu was not written by me, but by this young clerk. I ask for your guidance."

"You wrote this?" Lord Yan asked the young man, somewhat disbelieving. He looked like nothing more than a lad.

"In reply to your Excellency, I wrote it. I ask for Lord Yan's guidance."

Wei Zhuoqing was using this opportunity to recommend this talented young calligrapher to Yan Zhenqing.

Although he himself dreamed of being Lord Yan's student, he knew his own limitations. When he first saw the clerk's writing, he was astonished; the boy was a calligraphy prodigy! He immediately felt inferior.

However, he was not a petty man who envied talent. He wanted to cultivate this young clerk and help him find a mentor. That was why he had arranged for the clerk to deliver the menu.

Lord Yan looked at the menu in his hand, then at the young man. He understood Wei Zhuoqing’s painstaking efforts and his good intentions, and he felt inclined to take the student on.

The relationships between people are subtle; between friends or master and student, it often comes down to a sense of affinity.

Although the young clerk wore the most basic soldier's uniform, he possessed a quiet and refined temperament. The moment Yan Zhenqing saw him, he felt a fondness for him. He said to Wei Zhuoqing, "When I return, let him come along with me."

"Thank you, Lord Yan!" The young clerk immediately bowed to thank him and then withdrew.

After the clerk left, the officer on duty shouted, "Serve the cold dishes!"

The soldiers serving the food were all young men chosen for the task. They were beaming with joy as they served. Indeed, with wine to drink and meat to eat, who wouldn't be happy?

The soldiers served the dishes quickly.

Only then did Yan Zhenqing carefully examine the menu: eight cold dishes and sixteen hot dishes. All the ingredients were grown or raised by them; they had not touched the soldiers' food allowance or the silver in the granary.

Yan Zhenqing put the menu away. He knew that if Wei Zhuoqing had used the soldiers' food funds, they would be drinking thin air for the rest of the month after this feast.

This showed that Wei Zhuoqing’s ability to feed the soldiers so well meant their self-sufficient production was extraordinary. This practice could be promoted to other barracks.

In times of peace, soldiers were often bored and prone to causing trouble. It was better to have them engage in production, animal husbandry, and manual labor. This would enrich the soldiers' tables, reduce the burden on the imperial court, and decrease instability, three birds with one stone.

After the cold dishes were served, a young soldier brought over a jar of wine.

"What kind of good wine do you have here?" Lord Yan asked Wei Zhuoqing upon seeing the jar.

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "it is rice wine we brewed ourselves. Please, have a taste."

Hearing it was home-brewed, Lord Yan was delighted and asked, "Did you truly brew this yourselves?"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "it is indeed our own brew. Whether it is good or not, please taste it and you shall know."

"Good! If it is your own brew, we must drink it!" Lord Yan was very excited.

Wei Zhuoqing ordered that all the soldiers' cups be filled. Then, he stood up and said to everyone, "Everyone, raise your cups! Let us toast Lord Yan together!"

"A toast to Lord Yan!" All the soldiers stood up, raised their bowls, and shouted loudly.

Lord Yan also stood up happily, raised his large wine bowl, and shouted to the soldiers, "Bottoms up!"

The soldiers were thrilled. Whether veteran or recruit, none had ever drunk at the same table as an official of Lord Yan's stature. They shouted with all their might, "Bottoms up!"

The sound echoed through the granary, incredibly stirring and heartening. Lord Yan finished his wine and showed the bottom of the bowl to everyone.

The soldiers also finished their wine and showed their bowls to the Lord.

"Good!" Lord Yan shouted in approval.

This was the first time Yan Zhenqing had drunk from a large bowl and eaten meat with so many soldiers, and he was very excited.

"May I ask Lord Yan, how is the wine? Please give us your assessment," Wei Zhuoqing asked tentatively.

"Good wine! That you can brew such fine wine yourselves, I am very pleased!" Lord Yan loved wine; having served in the imperial court, what fine wine had he not tasted? He gave his full affirmation to the wine they had brewed.

"Thank you, my Lord!" the soldiers shouted in unison.

With Lord Yan's approval of their wine, a weight was lifted from Wei Zhuoqing's heart. The three major things he cared about had all been validated by Lord Yan, and he felt much more at ease.

What were these three major things?

The first was the issue of defense, which was Wei Zhuoqing’s primary concern upon taking office. Even in peacetime, he could not ignore it, so he had thoroughly resolved the defense issues upon arrival.

He had built the dam for two purposes: to strengthen defenses and to develop aquaculture, enriching the soldiers' lives, a move now affirmed by Lord Yan.

The second was the management of the granary. After Lord Yan carefully inspected every warehouse, he was very satisfied.

The third was the issue of agricultural and sideline production. Wei Zhuoqing had feared Lord Yan might think he was neglecting his duties. But as things stood, this too had received Lord Yan's approval.

With all three major matters affirmed, Wei Zhuoqing could finally drink in peace.

The eight cold dishes and the wine had been served. The soldiers responsible for serving were all young, handsome men chosen for the task. They moved in a line, entering one after another with trays. Seeing this, Lord Yan was pleased and said to Wei Zhuoqing, "You've only been here for a year, and you've done quite well!"

In the prosperous Tang Dynasty, formal occasions followed specific etiquette: after guests were seated, tea was served first, followed by cold dishes. Once the cold dishes were served, wine could be poured. After three rounds of wine, hot dishes were served.

The eight cold dishes were quickly finished, and the drinking began.

Yan Zhenqing carefully observed the eight cold dishes: a mix of meat and vegetables, each plate piled high and generous in portion. The chef was meticulous; the presentation and appearance of the dishes were excellent.

Every dish on the table was not only distinctive but also beautifully arranged.

For example, the "Red Oil Pork Skin Jelly." Lord Yan liked it the moment he saw it and ordered it to be placed in front of him.

How was this dish made? The chef boiled pig skin into a thick liquid, poured it into a clay basin to set, and once it had solidified into jelly, turned it out onto a large platter. He then carved it into a giant peony flower, sprinkled chopped red chili on the center, and drizzled it with sesame oil. It looked magnificent and festive.

Lord Yan was not only a great calligrapher but also a gourmet. Seeing this dish, he said to Wei Zhuoqing, "Your cook's knife skills are even more masterful than my calligraphy! This dish is a work of art; I truly cannot bear to use my chopsticks! Haha!"

"That our cook could receive such praise from Lord Yan is an honor for me. For this glory, I toast you with a bowl of wine."

"Bottoms up!" Lord Yan was very happy today. Everything he had seen during this inspection satisfied him, and his mood was excellent, making the drinking all the more enjoyable.

Wei Zhuoqing put down his wine and said to Yan Zhenqing, "Lord Yan, the rule at our granary table is that once the cold dishes are served, it signals the start of the feast. Please, Lord Yan, do the honors of 'cutting the ribbon' so the soldiers may begin."

"Very well!" Yan Zhenqing knew this rule, of course. If he didn't pick up his chopsticks, no one else dared to. He immediately picked up his chopsticks and took a piece of the pork skin jelly, effectively "cutting the ribbon."

Only then did the officer on duty shout, "Begin the feast!"

The soldiers shouted in unison, "Begin the feast!"

Instantly, the banquet became lively, and the granary was filled with the sound of chopsticks hitting plates. If Lord Yan hadn't been present, the sounds of finger-guessing games, drinking contests, and shouting would have lifted the roof. With Lord Yan there, no one dared to speak loudly.

Yan Zhenqing was truly happy today. He raised his wine to the soldiers and shouted, "This is the first time I, Yan Zhenqing, have drunk in such a grand setting. You have truly given me face. Everyone, fill your bowls, and let us have another!"

"Thank you, my Lord!" Everyone drank their wine together.

"Serve the hot dishes, 'Running Water Feast' style!" the officer on duty shouted.

The "Running Water Feast" originated in the Northwest during the Sui Dynasty and became popular in Henan and Hebei during the Tang. Its main feature was that every dish included broth, and as soon as one dish was finished, another was served, flowing like clouds and water, hence the name.

The first hot dish today was braised pork with potatoes, a traditional dish beloved by all.

A team of soldiers brought the dishes to the tables in large clay basins.

Yet, everyone still dared not use their chopsticks, all looking at Yan Zhenqing. This small gesture was enough to show that these soldiers were well-disciplined, and also that Wei Zhuoqing led them well.

Yan Zhenqing understood that everyone loved this dish, so he immediately took the first bite and said to them, "Don't be constrained, eat as you please!"

"Thank you, my Lord!" Following that, the sound of spoons and chopsticks clinking against bowls and basins filled the air.

After several hot dishes were served, it was time for the main course. The officer on duty shouted, "Bring out the main course; Roasted Whole Lamb!"

The main course arrived. The clerk and two soldiers carried a roasted whole lamb to Lord Yan: "Reporting to your Excellency: Roasted Whole Lamb, please do the honors!"

Yan Zhenqing saw that six soldiers were carrying three roasted lambs in total, more than enough for everyone.

Is this Wei Zhuoqing being too extravagant? Is he putting on a show for me? No. They didn't know I was coming to the granary beforehand. If I hadn't come, wouldn't they still be eating and drinking like this? It seems their self-sufficient production is truly impressive.

Thinking of this, Yan Zhenqing asked Wei Zhuoqing, "You have a main course? And it's roasted whole lamb! Haha, you eat better than I do in the city. Good! I don't just envy that you eat well; I approve of you ensuring the soldiers eat well. I shall do the honors!"

Lord Yan picked up a dagger and sliced a large piece of meat from the lamb's leg, which Wei Zhuoqing caught on a large platter.

"Haha! Even in the Imperial City, I haven't eaten roasted whole lamb. I am indebted to your hospitality, haha!" Although Lord Yan was a man of letters, he was infected by the rugged and hearty atmosphere here.

"Lord Yan has done the honors, everyone, eat to your heart's content!" Wei Zhuoqing told the soldiers, meaning for them to relax.

As the roasted lamb passed by each soldier, everyone cut off a piece of meat, and everyone ate with great relish.

Lord Yan tasted a piece of the roasted lamb and felt the flavor was extraordinary. It was roasted perfectly, crispy on the outside, tender on the inside, and well-seasoned. It was not the work of an ordinary cook.

He asked Wei Zhuoqing curiously, "Lord Wei, do you have a culinary master here?"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "one of our cooks had parents who ran a barbecue shop. He has been learning to roast lamb since he was a child. Roasted whole lamb is his specialty. How does it taste, my Lord?"

"Your cook is a true master. This roasted whole lamb has both flavor and presentation. Good!" Yan Zhenqing could not stop praising the main course. He had never expected such delicious food to be made in a granary.

Wei Zhuoqing's predecessor had only cared about lining his own pockets and ignored the soldiers' lives. Every time Yan Zhenqing visited, he saw soldiers eating food without meat or oil, and the soldiers were full of resentment, often deserting.

Because the granary was an enclave within the city, a bit far away, Yan Zhenqing couldn't reach it easily, which gave those corrupt officials their chance.

Wei Zhuoqing's arrival had changed everything, putting Yan Zhenqing completely at ease. Previously, he had often lost sleep over this granary.

Seeing all the officers and soldiers looking so happy and high-spirited, Yan Zhenqing knew they were content under Wei Zhuoqing's management, and that Wei Zhuoqing loved his soldiers like his own children.

Yan Zhenqing’s drinking was just to keep up appearances; his goal was to truly understand the soldiers' lives. He truly couldn't believe everything he was seeing.

He re-examined his purpose for coming and the process of his inspection. First, Wei Zhuoqing had no prior knowledge of his visit, of this, he was certain.

Second, even if Wei Zhuoqing were putting on a show, he would need a substantial material foundation to do so.

He thought to himself: Such a good official, forced by the Yang family to be separated from his own flesh and blood, with nowhere to hide; it is truly outrageous!

A banquet like this, held every half-month... If he didn't have a solid foundation, he wouldn't dare be this extravagant; he is a cautious man. In just over a year, he has turned a granary that once caused me such anxiety into something so vibrant. This Wei Zhuoqing is no simple man. It seems I did not misjudge him.

The more Yan Zhenqing thought, the happier he became. He couldn't help but raise his wine again and say to the soldiers, "Seeing you eating meat and drinking wine under Lord Wei's leadership, I am very gratified. Those who haven't filled their bowls, fill them quickly! Let us raise our cups together and drink to having such a good official as Lord Wei!"

"Bottoms up!" the soldiers shouted loudly.

chapters.title: Gao Lishi Intends to Help
chapters.content:
The atmosphere at the dining table became more lively, though everyone remained somewhat reserved with Magistrate Yan present.

Yan Zhenqing set down his wine bowl and said to the group, "Do not feel embarrassed to eat your fill just because I am here. Eat! Let us all eat!" Infected by the soldiers' high spirits, Yan Zhenqing used a dagger to spear a large piece of roasted mutton and began to eat.

Seeing that their superior was doing the same, the soldiers forgot the etiquette Wei Zhuoqing had previously taught them and began to gorge themselves.

The officers took turns offering toasts to Magistrate Yan and his entourage, serving them food, and the scene was one of harmony and joy.

It was the first time Yan Zhenqing had drunk with over a hundred soldiers at one large table. The scene was not only grand and lively, but it also bridged the distance between the official and his men. Consequently, he drank with great pleasure.

Yan Zhenqing was very familiar with this granary and its surrounding environment; there was indeed much good land. He asked Wei Zhuoqing, "Have you reclaimed all the land around the stream?"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "Yes, sir. I saw so much fertile land, all irrigated, lying fallow, and I felt it was a great pity."

"My ancestors also had a few acres of land, but none were as fertile as this. So, I had the soldiers reclaim all of it to make the best use of the soil."

"This year is the first year, so the yield is not high, but it is enough for our own consumption. Next year, I will have to request your approval to build two more warehouses; otherwise, if we have a bumper harvest, there will be nowhere to store the grain."

"You want to build two more warehouses? Are you certain?"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "I have calculated that the grain we grew ourselves this year has already made up for the previous deficit in the granary. Without more warehouses next year, there will be no place to store the harvest."

"I can approve the construction of two more granaries, but I have no silver to give you for it. The saying that 'a clever wife cannot cook without rice' is a truth at any time and in any place!"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "This mountain is full of treasures. If we need timber, there is timber; if we need earth and stone, there is earth and stone. As long as Magistrate Yan approves our construction, we do not need a single coin from you."

"You can build two granaries without silver?" Yan Zhenqing was a bit skeptical.

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "We have plenty of young, strong labor, and they are all excellent men. They can kill enemies with swords and spears, till the land with hoes, and work with tools. With these men and this mountain, building a few granaries is no problem."

"Good! Since you can do it without the imperial treasury's silver, I approve the construction of two more granaries!" Yan Zhenqing was naturally happy to approve anything that didn't cost him money. As long as no silver was required, he would support it wholeheartedly.

Wei Zhuoqing was single-mindedly focused on the development of the granary, treating it as his home, and Magistrate Yan naturally trusted him.

"However," Magistrate Yan continued, "this is a vital granary; there must be no negligence. Not needing silver while adding two granaries is certainly a good thing, but do not forget your primary duties."

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "From now on, you will never see a mouse in our granary, nor will you find a single grain of moldy food." This was Wei Zhuoqing's bottom line for managing the granary.

"That is excellent. With you at the granary, I can sleep soundly when I return."

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "Magistrate Yan not only took me in during my time of distress, saving my family from the clutches of the tyrant Yang, but also arranged such a wonderful place for me, a veritable paradise on earth. It is like a fish finding water."

"If nothing unexpected happens, I shall spend the rest of my days here. I have a belly full of gratitude, but I do not know where to begin. All my words are concentrated in this bowl of wine; I will drink first as a sign of respect!"

"Good, bottoms up!" After finishing the bowl, Magistrate Yan said to Wei Zhuoqing, "This is a trivial matter; do not mention it again. If you manage the granary well for me, you have done me a great service. I approve of you spending your retirement here."

"The granary is now in your hands. Whatever you do here is fine, but when the imperial court requires grain, you must guarantee the supply."

"Please rest assured, Excellency. I guarantee: as long as I am in the granary for a day, the grain will be there for a day."

Hearing this, Magistrate Yan felt even more at ease.

The two men spoke very congenially, while the soldiers seized the time to eat and drink.

The next day, Wei Zhuoqing accompanied Magistrate Yan to inspect the mountain land outside the granary, the stream, and the vast tracts of newly reclaimed fields.

Seeing so much new land, Yan Zhenqing realized that without two more granaries, there would certainly be nowhere to store the grain after the autumn harvest.

Looking at the pigsties, sheep pens, and flocks of chickens and ducks, Yan Zhenqing asked curiously, "You have only been at the granary for a little over a year; where did you get so many pigs, sheep, chickens, and ducks?"

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "Our mountain is full of wild produce, timber, and medicinal herbs. I have the soldiers take them to the city to trade with the commoners. The piglets, lambs, chicks, and ducklings we get in return grow up in just a few months."

By the end of the inspection, Yan Zhenqing had a comprehensive understanding of Wei Zhuoqing and could not help but look at this magistrate who had come to seek his protection with new eyes. He might not necessarily be a great magistrate, but he was certainly a highly competent granary manager.

When seeing Magistrate Yan off at the mountain pass, he specifically went to look at the small reservoir.

The location Wei Zhuoqing chose to build the dam was very clever; below the dam was the first defensive pass. If the dam were opened, anyone at the first pass would be washed away. And once the mountain road was flooded, it would be nothing but mud, making it impossible for anyone to climb up. Only then did Yan Zhenqing realize that Wei Zhuoqing was also a man who knew how to use military strategy.

Wei Zhuoqing saw Yan Zhenqing to the mountain pass and handed him a cart of mountain goods: "Magistrate Yan, this is a cart of local produce, wild mushrooms, dates, walnuts, and some dried and salted chicken, duck, fish, and meat. Please take them back for the soldiers in the city to taste."

"What is in those jars?" Yan Zhenqing asked, noticing several jars on the cart.

"In reply to your Excellency," Wei Zhuoqing said, "There is a jar of honey and three jars of rice wine we brewed ourselves."

"Good, I will accept it all." Yan Zhenqing never accepted gifts from his subordinates, but he accepted these. On the way back, he thought the whole time that Gaoqing had recommended a capable general to him, and he would have to invite him for a drink to show his gratitude.

Beyond the Helan Mountains on the northwestern frontier lay the vast grasslands where the Turks and other ethnic minorities roamed. Although Emperor Gaozong of Tang, Li Zhi, had destroyed the Eastern and Western Turkic Khanates, the descendants of the Turks remained. They continued to multiply, and their population and livestock grew, forming several tribes.

The Turks were hardy and capable, with robust bodies, great strength, excellent martial arts, and were skilled in riding and archery. They possessed great endurance; after a full meal, they could endure hunger for three days while fighting continuously.

In grassland warfare, every Turkic man was a brave and fierce warrior. They upheld the spirit of fighting to the death rather than surrendering. Among the many ethnic minorities in the northwest, the Turks were the formidable rivals of the Tang frontier garrisons.

Twenty miles outside Muzi Mountain, there was a Turkic tribe with a population of over 100,000. They had organized a cavalry force of 2,000 men. They frequently crossed Muzi Mountain, penetrated deep into Tang territory, killed frontier residents, and plundered their livestock and property, becoming a major scourge of the Tang border.

General Guo Ziyi sent his beloved lieutenant, Zhao Shan, to lead 1,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry to camp at Muzi Mountain. Relying on the natural barrier, they blocked the repeated incursions of the tribes and secured the safety of this Tang frontier fortress.

However, after the beginning of autumn, the temperature around Muzi Mountain dropped continuously as a cold wave hit. The soldiers guarding the frontier were still wearing summer uniforms. With winter approaching, the lack of padded winter robes became a major problem for the troops.

Zhao Shan himself felt the weather getting colder, and like everyone else, he had no winter clothing to add.

"My stomach hurts whenever I get cold, and once it hurts, I get diarrhea immediately." Deputy General Li Hu was a 50-year-old veteran, and like many old men, he suffered from the cold. He was worried about how to solve the problem of winter robes.

"General Guo has already reported our winter situation to the imperial court. Don't worry, there will be a result soon," Zhao Shan said to Li Hu.

The biggest difference between the weather in the great northwest and the interior was the large temperature difference between day and night. Once the northwest wind blew in the middle of the night, soldiers on guard duty without padded robes would be unable to endure the cold, and there had even been cases of soldiers freezing to death.

"Let's gather all the padded robes in the camp and provide them to the soldiers on night guard duty; the others will have to find another way." Li Hu was in charge of logistics and military supplies. Without silver from the court, he could not obtain cloth or cotton to make robes, leaving the soldiers to suffer the cold.

As it grew colder, the soldiers thought of their own ways to keep warm. One soldier named Chen Huiguang, nearly six and a half feet tall (equivalent to 1.9 meters today), was robust and strong as an ox, wielding a Green Dragon Crescent Blade with immense power. His only weakness was that he feared the cold.

He had a fellow villager and friend named Zhao Si, thin as a monkey and nicknamed "Skinny Monkey." Like Chen Huiguang, he was also very afraid of the cold. As it got colder, the two discussed going up the mountain to cut wild grass, drying it to weave into mats to use as bedding. By lighting charcoal fires inside their tents, it wouldn't be so cold.

Seeing their method was effective, others also went up the mountain to cut grass. A few soldiers wove some mats and gave them to the commander, Zhao Shan. He thought the mats were excellent, rewarded those soldiers with a bowl of wine each, and called on all troops to go up the mountain to cut grass and weave mats. He also had the families accompanying the army sew coats from the pelts of yellow sheep, wolves, and wild rabbits obtained from hunting for the soldiers on guard duty.

However, the vast majority of soldiers could only huddle around fires in their tents to keep warm.

Just before the first heavy snow of Muzi Mountain, Emperor Xuanzong sent people to deliver padded robes, hats, trousers, and boots. The Muzi Mountain camp erupted in cheers.

The soldiers put on the warm padded robes and shouted in unison, "Long live, long live, long live the Emperor!"

The extra-large robe that Wei Ziyun had specially sewn could not be worn by anyone, eventually falling to Chen Huiguang. When he tried it on, it fit perfectly, as if it had been tailored for him.

Emperor Xuanzong also allocated a sum of silver for them to purchase cotton and cloth locally, allowing the soldiers' families to sew winter bedding for them.

However, the silver allocated by the court was far from enough, due to the layers of "skimming" by officials; by the time the silver reached Muzi Mountain, half was already gone. The winter clothing for the soldiers and their families remained a major problem.

Chen Huiguang's padded robe was too large, and "Skinny Monkey" could use it as a quilt. Before the new quilts were issued, Skinny Monkey often slept under Chen Huiguang's robe.

One day, Zhao Si discovered something in the collar of Chen Huiguang's robe. The two tore open the collar and found a note inside.

Chen Huiguang, who was literate, opened the note and saw a short poem: "Muzi Mountain, Muzi Mountain, Tang soldiers guard the frontier. Heaven and earth are cold, swords and blades are freezing, the Emperor sends warmth in the form of robes. Adding more thread and cotton, who will wear this extra-large robe? I regret this life, for we have no fate; I shall wait for you in the human world in the next life."

Chen Huiguang and Skinny Monkey realized it was a love poem written by a palace maid. The content was very clear, and this was no small matter. Anyone caught having private correspondence with a palace maid would be beheaded!

Chen Huiguang dared not hide it, let alone keep the note. He immediately reported it to his centurion, who reported it to his superiors. Finally, the note reached Zhao Shan. Just as a supply convoy was about to return to Chang'an, he handed the note to the convoy manager and wrote a letter to General Guo Ziyi, specifically stating that Chen Huiguang had nothing to do with the matter.

Upon seeing the note and Zhao Shan's letter, Guo Ziyi dared not handle it on his own. He handed the palace maid's note and the general's letter to the great eunuch, Gao Lishi.

When Gao Lishi saw it, he was shocked! A palace maid daring to communicate privately with the outside world and seduce a frontier soldier; he said to General Guo Ziyi, "These palace maids are outrageous; this is a capital offense! What is to be done? The palace is heavily guarded; how did this little maid manage to send the note out?"

"The Eunuch may not know, but this note was sewn into the collar of a padded robe and brought out of the palace. The soldier who received this robe is named Chen Huiguang, and he has been stationed at the Muzi Mountain fortress; he has never had any contact with any palace maid." Guo Ziyi was worried about his soldier being implicated.

"Judging by the poem written by the palace maid, this matter has nothing to do with your soldier. This maid is too bold; she is simply lawless!"

Gao Lishi had spent most of his life in the palace, and this was the first time he had encountered such a thing. He was shocked and worried for the ignorant and daring maid. Such a matter could be handled by the Chief of the Inner Palace with a single word, without needing to alarm the Emperor.

However, Guo Ziyi wanted to save the maid's life. He knew that if the note were handed to the Inner Palace female officials, the maid would certainly be killed. To an Inner Palace official, killing a maid was as easy as killing a wild cat.

If the note were presented to the Emperor, who was the most benevolent ruler of the day, perhaps the maid might be spared.

Thinking of this, Guo Ziyi said to Gao Lishi, "General Gao (Gao Lishi had been titled General of the Flying Cavalry during Xuanzong's reign) has always been known for his compassion. Please, General, plead for mercy before the Emperor for this little maid and spare her life."

"In such matters, how dare we servants say too much before the Emperor? Don't look at us as if we are important when we are delivering imperial edicts to you; in front of the Emperor, we don't even dare to breathe loudly." Gao Lishi was speaking the truth.

"Will the General hand the note to the Inner Palace female officials, or present it to the Emperor?" General Guo asked tentatively.

"This maid is indeed too bold, but I do not want her to die either. I will present it to the Emperor. Li Taibai has entered the palace these past few days, and the Emperor and the Imperial Consort are very happy. Perhaps if the Emperor is in a good mood, he will grant an extra favor and let this little maid go." Gao Lishi said this only to give General Guo face.

chapters.title: Miracles Are Created by the Son of Heaven
chapters.content:
Gao Lishi, with the poem written by Wei Ziyun tucked inside his robe, arrived at the palace where the Emperor and Consort Yang were drinking and enjoying the festivities. The dancing girls had just finished a routine.

This was a new dance, with lyrics by Li Bai, music by Li Guinian, and choreography by Consort Yang. Emperor Xuanzong had watched it and offered nothing but praise.

Seeing the Emperor in high spirits, Gao Lishi presented the poem: "Reporting to Your Majesty, General Guo Ziyi has submitted a poem written by a palace maid for the soldiers on the frontier."

"Oh? Is that so? As for the poem, let Master Taibai take a look first."

"As you command, Your Majesty." Gao Lishi delivered the poem into Li Bai’s hands.

Li Bai had already consumed quite a bit of wine and was in a state of excitement. Upon hearing it was a poem written by a palace maid for frontier soldiers, he became interested. He took it from Gao Lishi, read it, and laughed heartily: "A fine poem! A truly fine poem!"

"Since the Master calls it a fine poem, why not recite it for us to hear?" Consort Yang, hearing it was written by a young palace maid, also became intrigued.

Li Bai glanced at the Emperor, who nodded in approval.

Li Bai recited: "Muci Mountain, Muci Mountain, the Tang soldiers guard the frontier pass. The world is cold, the swords are frigid, our Emperor’s battle robe sends warmth. Adding more thread, adding more cotton, who can wear this oversized battle robe? I hate that in this life, we have no chance to meet; I shall wait for you in the human world in the next life."

Upon hearing this, Emperor Xuanzong realized: isn't this singing the praises of his decree for the ladies of the six palaces to sew cotton battle robes for the frontier soldiers?

He said to Li Guinian, "Set this poem to music; it will sound even better when sung."

"I obey the decree." Li Guinian immediately composed the music and ordered the musicians to perform it, with himself singing the solo.

Gao Lishi observed the Emperor’s expression from the side, sweating for the daring little palace maid. Her life and death hung entirely on the Emperor’s mood.

Li Guinian was indeed a genius musician of the Great Tang, a brilliant composer, in modern terms.

He improvised the melody and sang it with such moving, delicate grace that when he reached the line, "I hate that in this life, we have no chance to meet; I shall wait for you in the human world in the next life," he was moved to tears, and Consort Yang followed suit. Emperor Xuanzong, a romantic monarch who understood poetry and rhythm better than anyone, couldn't help but praise: "A fine poem and a fine melody!"

Gao Lishi was like a tapeworm in the Emperor’s stomach; he understood the Emperor’s mind better than anyone and knew how to act according to his wishes. That was why, ever since the reign of Wu Zetian, he had been highly favored by the Emperor.

Seeing the Emperor happy, he immediately asked, "Reporting to Your Majesty, how should we deal with that frontier soldier? General Guo is awaiting the imperial decree."

Gao Lishi did not mention Wei Ziyun, but the frontier soldier and Wei Ziyun were one and the same matter. How the Emperor would deal with them depended entirely on his current mood.

"My two beloved subjects, one of you recited the poem and the other composed the music; how do you think we should deal with this palace maid and this soldier?" Emperor Xuanzong asked Li Bai and Li Guinian.

Li Bai immediately replied, "Reporting to Your Majesty, I believe this poem has nothing to do with the frontier soldier. He received this poem purely by chance, or one might say, it was fate in this life. However, I fear they are destined to have the connection but not the opportunity in this lifetime."

"Whether they have the opportunity or not is not for you or me to decide," Li Guinian interjected. "Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven. If the Son of Heaven says they have a connection, they have it; if the Son of Heaven says they have the opportunity, they have it. Everything in our human world must obey the Son of Heaven!"

Li Guinian’s words saved Wei Ziyun. Emperor Xuanzong was very pleased with what he heard and immediately asked Gao Lishi, "High Official Gao, have you found this palace maid who wrote the poem?"

"Reporting to Your Majesty, I have not yet received the decree, so I have not searched for her."

"Pass on my decree: find this palace maid immediately. I grant her amnesty and shall fulfill their miraculous fate in this life," Emperor Xuanzong commanded.

"Thank you for your immense grace! Long live the Emperor, long live, long live!"

The Consort, Li Bai, Li Guinian, and Gao Lishi all knelt to thank the Emperor.

The Emperor had not only pardoned the palace maid but also intended to fulfill their fate. This was something Gao Lishi had never expected.

Feeling both excited and flustered, he knelt before the Emperor and said, "Your servant obeys the decree. On behalf of this little girl, I thank Your Majesty for your great mercy in fulfilling this miraculous fate between two people. This story will surely be passed down for generations to come."

As Gao Lishi was about to leave, Consort Yang stopped him: "General Gao, a palace maid's marriage cannot be too shabby. Go to my quarters later and take some silks, fine fabrics, and gold and silver jewelry to give her as a dowry."

After saying this, the Consort looked at Emperor Xuanzong, who nodded in agreement.

Gao Lishi immediately replied, "Your servant will strictly follow the Consort’s decree. Long live the Consort!"

Gao Lishi received the imperial decree and immediately went to the various palaces to find the maid who wrote the poem. Three days passed, and there were no leads.

Having failed to find her in three days, Gao Lishi was very anxious. If no one admitted to it, how could he answer to the Emperor? What was he to do?

This was the first time Gao Lishi had encountered a difficulty while working for the Emperor. He sent out his capable subordinates and repeated the Emperor’s decree countless times, but no one dared to admit to writing the poem.

Gao Lishi strolled into Xingqing Palace and called all the managers and eunuchs together, questioning them over and over again. They all claimed that the maids under their supervision had never written any such poem.

As soon as Gao Lishi left, Xiaoyue said to Foreman Yan, "It seems Wei Ziyun made an extra-large cotton battle robe, and she also wrote some poem..."

"Shut up!" Before Xiaoyue could finish, Foreman Yan interrupted her: "Do you still want your reward money?"

"I do! Xiaoyue dreams of getting the reward money."

"If you give Wei Ziyun away and she leaves Xingqing Palace, and Master Yang doesn't get her, you can forget about it!"

"That's right, I was muddled, damn me!" Xiaoyue lacked Foreman Yan’s cunning and didn't think as far ahead.

Thus, the two of them kept their mouths shut, ensuring Wei Ziyun’s secret remained hidden, and Gao Lishi could never find the palace maid who wrote the poem.

With three thousand women in the harem, it was impossible for Gao Lishi to question every single one. Just as he was pacing in circles with anxiety, his old friend, Eunuch Gong, came to find him.

"Have you found the palace maid who wrote the poem?" Eunuch Gong asked, seeing Gao Lishi’s anxious state.

"I’ve asked all six palaces and repeated the Emperor’s decree countless times, but no one dares to admit it."

"I fear someone knows but is deliberately not saying."

"Hmm? Who is so bold as to defy an imperial decree?" This was something Gao Lishi hadn't considered. No wonder he couldn't find her; someone was deliberately hiding it.

"If you arrest Foreman Yan and Xiaoyue and interrogate them, you will know."

"Bring Yan Jiao and Xiaoyue here at once!" Gao Lishi ordered.

Several eunuchs immediately brought Foreman Yan and Xiaoyue before Gao Lishi.

"This servant pays respects to Lord Gao!"

"You two have a lot of nerve!" Gao Lishi roared.

"This servant does not know what crime I have committed," Yan Jiao said, still stubborn.

"Do you know why I have called you here?"

"This servant knows, but I truly do not know who wrote the poem." Yan Jiao thought, If I don't say anything, what can you do to me?

"You don't know? Fine, take them out!" Gao Lishi ordered.

The two eunuchs dragged Foreman Yan out. Xiaoyue, left behind, was scared to death. She immediately said to Gao Lishi, "This servant deserves to die! I only heard a bit of gossip and wasn't sure, and Foreman Yan told me not to say anything."

"Now that you have spoken, I grant you amnesty."

"Thank you, Lord Gao! I will tell you everything."

"Get up and speak. Tell me everything you know. If you hide anything else, I will not be lenient."

"Thank you, Lord Gao! Under Foreman Yan, there are three girls who wash the night-soil buckets. One of them is named Wei Ziyun. Master Yang Guoguang took a fancy to her and wanted to take her as a concubine. But she refused, so she was sent into the palace to be a maid."

"Is this Yang Guoguang a relative of Prime Minister Yang?" Gao Lishi asked.

"Reporting to you, my Lord," Xiaoyue said, "exactly. After he learned Wei Ziyun had become a palace maid, he bribed Foreman Yan to torture her. He planned to step in later as a 'good person' to get her out of the palace, so that Wei Ziyun would be grateful and agree to be his concubine."

"How did they torture Wei Ziyun?" Gao Lishi asked with concern.

"Reporting to you, my Lord," Xiaoyue said, "they didn't manage to do anything to her; instead, they were tortured by her until they were miserable."

"Hmm?" Gao Lishi found this strange. "Isn't Wei Ziyun a lowly maid? How could she torture Foreman Yan? Tell me in detail!"

"Reporting to you, my Lord," Xiaoyue said immediately, "at first, Ziyun was very obedient. She would wash 200 buckets a day by herself, and she endured Foreman Yan’s beatings and abuse. Later, when she found out Master Yang wanted to take her as a concubine, she didn't take it anymore."

"As a little maid, wasn't she just meat on your chopping block, to be bullied as you pleased?" Gao Lishi knew the palace too well.

"Reporting to you, my Lord, this little maid is not ordinary. She knows martial arts. She first knocked Foreman Yan to the ground. Foreman Yan called five or six strong women to surround her, but she knocked them all down too. She even assigned work to those women, making them wash all the buckets while she acted as the supervisor."

"Haha, interesting. So many women couldn't beat her?" Gao Lishi became even more interested in Wei Ziyun, believing she was capable of such a rebellious act.

"Reporting to you, my Lord, if I hadn't seen it with my own eyes, I wouldn't believe it either. They told me to be a 'good person' and persuade Ziyun to agree to Master Yang, so she didn't beat me."

"I have also seen it; those women go to wash the buckets every day," Eunuch Gong added.

"Haha, the Emperor and the Consort will be very happy to hear this. Go and bring Ziyun here." Gao Lishi had found Wei Ziyun and felt relieved. Otherwise, he wouldn't have been able to answer to the Emperor.

He wanted to see what kind of person this Wei Ziyun was to be so formidable. A tiny maid daring to knock down a foreman and make them do her work; this was something he had never heard of before.

Eunuch Gong went to the courtyard where Wei Ziyun and the others washed the buckets. Several burly women were washing, nearly finished, while Wei Ziyun sat to the side supervising them. Seeing this, Eunuch Gong couldn't help but want to laugh.
